title: Grindhouse
full_review:
"Grindhouse" (Dimension) is a cinematically inventive but brutally sordid two-part homage to the cheapie exploitation films of the 1960s and '70s.

It's actually two films for the price of one, and in Europe they are in fact being released separately in longer versions.

The first is writer-director Robert Rodriguez's zombie-inspired "Planet Terror." Survivors in a plague-infested Texas town -- the mysterious Wray (Freddy Rodriguez), go-go dancer Cherry (Rose McGowan) and anesthesiologist Dakota (Marley Shelton) among them -- face down mutants run amok. Along the way, Cherry loses her leg, and Wray must fit her with a machine-gun prosthetic device, a novel twist to be sure! As if that weren't enough, Josh Brolin plays Dr. Block, Dakota's estranged husband, who is trying to kill her at every turn.

Then, writer-director Quentin Tarantino's revenge slasher "Death Proof" focuses on a sadistic killer known as Stuntman Mike (Kurt Russell) who stalks frank-talking girlfriends Arlene (Vanessa Ferlito), Jungle Julia (Sydney Poitier) and Shanna (Jordan Ladd), with a horrific outcome, and then makes the mistake of targeting a group of movie stuntwomen, Abernathy (Rosario Dawson), Kim (Tracie Thoms) and real-life stunt person Zoe Bell, this time, getting more than he bargained for.

It must be said that the car sequences in Tarantino's film are thrillingly executed.

Furthermore, the film is wittily packaged to give the experience of what it was like to go to a second-run movie theater in those days, complete with coming attractions, messages from the "theater management" and other hallmarks of the unlamented genre. Since film prints in those theaters were pretty worn, there are intentional streaks and scratches here.

Both halves benefit from solid performances (including cameos by the likes of Bruce Willis), and there's no denying that each has been made with consummate skill, as are the spot-on, sleazy "trailers" which frame the features. Tarantino's dialogue for his tough-talking young women really crackles, but goes overboard with vulgarity and frank sex talk.

Unfortunately, all the unsavory elements that made those original B-movies so objectionable in the first place are now presented with a permissiveness that far eclipses the originals.

The film contains pervasive rough language and profanity, heavy-duty gore with bloodshed and worse, blatant sexuality including upper female nudity and attempted rape, a nongraphic encounter with partial nudity, sadism, innuendo, torture, much gross-out imagery and vigilante justice. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
